title: Doomscrolling: Why do we do it?
reason: 从昨日的职场与团队管理轮换到软件和数字生活、生产力主题。节目解释人们为何会持续浏览负面信息，适合联系平台告警、行业资讯和信息过载等熟悉场景；练习反复调用六个高频表达，从原文支撑的回忆逐步过渡到改写、受限工作场景应用和有限自由表达。

targetExpressions.meaning: feel a strong need or pressure to do something
targetExpressions.usage: During an incident, engineers may feel compelled to check every new alert.
Try to seek out reliable information before making a decision.

targetExpressions.meaning: easily available whenever you want it
targetExpressions.usage: With notifications on tap, it is easy to keep checking your phone.

targetExpressions.meaning: notice or concentrate on someone or something
targetExpressions.usage: A project lead should pay attention to risks without ignoring progress.

targetExpressions.meaning: compensate for something bad or missing with something good
targetExpressions.usage: One quiet evening can help make up for a stressful day.

targetExpressions.meaning: describe something as better or more attractive than it really is
targetExpressions.usage: We should not romanticise constant overtime as proof of commitment.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: In the programme, what does it mean to feel compelled to look at bad news?

options.text: To feel a strong need or pressure to look at it.
To be unable to understand it.
To be paid to report it.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The transcript says people feel compelled to look at and even seek out bad news, meaning they feel a strong urge to do it.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the transcript-based phrase: Some people actively ______ bad news, even when it makes them feel worse.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Neil says people may 'seek out' bad news, and Ella similarly says that people go searching out for it.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: If news is 'on tap' on our phones, what does that mean?

options.text: It is easily available whenever we want it.
It is checked by an editor once a week.
It is limited to local events.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: Sam defines 'on tap' as easily available in whatever amount you want, whenever you want.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the explanation of negativity bias: Humans naturally ______ the negative stuff.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: The transcript says humans naturally pay attention to negative information because recognising danger was vital to survival.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Why might humans naturally focus on negative information, according to the programme?

options.text: Noticing dangers helped our ancestors survive.
Negative stories were easier to write.
People in caves received global news alerts.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The programme links negativity bias to survival: our ancestors needed to know about dangers and avoid them.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete Ella's point: The little good news we hear does not ______ all the depressing news.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Ella says the good news does not make up for the bad news; the programme defines the phrase as compensating for something bad with something good.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: What does Clara suggest society may do with traumatic experiences?

options.text: Make them sound better or more valuable than they really are.
Remove them completely from the news.
Treat them only as local information.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: Clara says trauma is romanticised, and Sam explains that this means making something sound better than it really is.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the reusable digital-habit sentence: With breaking news ______, it is easy to keep checking your phone.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: This lightly transfers the transcript's description of 24/7 news being on tap on our phones.

assessment.retellingPrompt: Retell the episode in 80-120 words without looking at the full transcript. Use this structure: (1) topic - what doomscrolling is and why constant news makes it possible; (2) two key ideas - negativity bias and the difference between local news in the past and global news today; (3) conclusion or example - the emotional effect of too much bad news. Phrase bank: 'seek out', 'on tap', 'make up for'. Use at least two phrases naturally. Simple, clear English is enough; advanced vocabulary and complex sentences are not required.
referencePoints: Doomscrolling means spending a lot of time reading negative news stories on a phone or computer.
People around the world may feel compelled to look at and even seek out bad news.
The internet and the non-stop news cycle make large amounts of news available on tap.
Negativity bias may come from human evolution because noticing danger was important for survival.
Early humans mainly knew local dangers, while people today receive bad news from all over the world.
The limited good news may not make up for depressing news, and romanticising trauma can strengthen the focus on negative experiences.
